analysis.one_liner: Rolls back Clean Water Act permits for farm runoff, stormwater, and wetlands development.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Clean Water rollback 240-185 in May 1995, but the Senate never voted and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 961 would rewrite the Clean Water Act: it drops federal permits for most stormwater runoff and for land-applied livestock manure, requires taxpayers to compensate landowners when wetland protections cut a property's value, stretches city sewer-cleanup deadlines to as long as 15 years, and blocks any new water rule costing $25 million or more a year unless the EPA certifies it maximizes net benefits. It also funds wastewater grants for small rural towns, Alaska villages, and border colonias. The House passed it 240-185 on May 16, 1995, but the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee never reported it, and it died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large livestock operations, real estate developers and landowners, industrial dischargers, and cities facing sewer-cleanup deadlines gain the most: manure and stormwater lose their permit requirements, wetland restrictions become compensable takings, and compliance clocks stretch out. Rural towns, Alaska villages, and border colonias would gain wastewater construction grants and easier loan terms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large farms, developers, and industrial dischargers

how_it_helps.text: Removes livestock manure applied to land from the point-source permit program and keeps concentrated animal feeding operation waste lagoons out of the waters the Act regulates, with existing lagoons exempt regardless of size.

Repeals the municipal and industrial stormwater permit provisions and excludes stormwater from the definition of a 'point source,' replacing federal permits with state-run programs the states largely design.

Requires the federal government to compensate property owners when wetland protections diminish a property's fair market value by 20 percent or more, and to buy the land at fair market value at the owner's option when the loss exceeds 50 percent.
Lets cities stretch combined and separate sewer overflow compliance schedules to 15 years and rewrites existing court consent decrees and EPA orders to match the new, longer timetables.

Bars new regulatory requirements or guidance under the Act that would cost $25 million or more a year unless the Administrator certifies the rule maximizes net benefits, and requires risk assessments before most standards.
Lets states set their own schedules for total maximum daily load cleanup plans and judge their own 'reasonable progress,' with full attainment pushed to December 31, 2015.

Funds wastewater treatment grants for small rural communities of 3,000 or fewer people, rural and Native Alaska villages, Great Lakes sediment cleanup, Chesapeake Bay programs, and border colonias, and eases loan repayment for disadvantaged communities.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the new wetland compensation and buyout obligations and the wastewater grants. Swimmers, anglers, and communities downstream of farms, cities, and industrial sites would absorb the cost of unpermitted stormwater and manure runoff and delayed sewer fixes, in the form of dirtier beaches, streams, and drinking-water sources.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and people who use public waters

drawbacks.text: Stormwater and manure runoff, major sources of the pollution that closes beaches and feeds algal blooms, would no longer need federal permits, shifting the cost of that pollution to swimmers, fishermen, and downstream water users.
The wetland compensation and buyout duties are open-ended liabilities paid from federal coffers whenever regulation reduces a property's value by a fifth or more.
Stretching combined sewer overflow compliance to 15 years and rewriting existing court-ordered cleanup deadlines defers sewage overflows into rivers and harbors rather than ending them.
States could set their own cleanup schedules under the total maximum daily load program and count expected future pollution controls toward today's targets, delaying attainment to as late as 2015.
The bill repeals the requirement that the federal government cover half the cost of wastewater projects in border colonias, poor communities that often lack any sewer service.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill answers real complaints: cities faced genuinely expensive combined-sewer obligations, and rural towns lacked basic wastewater service. Its grant programs and loan flexibility for small and poor communities have real value. But the dominant effect is deregulation — unpermitted runoff, compensable wetland protections, 15-year sewer timelines, and a cost-benefit veto over new standards — whose costs do not disappear but transfer to the public as dirtier water and deferred cleanup. On balance it serves regulated interests and development more than the people who drink, swim in, and fish the nation's waters.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 240-185 in May 1995, but the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee never reported it and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 240-185 on May 16, 1995, with 195 of 230 Republicans in favor and only 45 of 203 Democrats.
A Democratic motion to send the bill back to committee with instructions failed 169-256 the same day, with 159 of 203 Democrats voting for it and 219 of 230 Republicans against.
The Senate received the bill on May 18, 1995 and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works; the record shows no further action.
The bill text was printed as received in the Senate, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 without the Senate ever voting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Clean Water Act rules in force in 1995 stayed in place — so people who swim, fish, or drink from the nation's waters are better off than they would have been under the rollback. The industries and cities that wanted looser rules got nothing, though they also avoided the bill's new taxpayer-funded compensation obligations becoming a template.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Anyone who swims, fishes, or drinks tap water

for.name: Bud Shuster
for.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, steered it through committee (reported 42-16), and managed it to passage on the House floor 240-185.

for.name: 195 of 230 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage on May 16, 1995.

for.name: Agriculture, development, and manufacturing industry coalition
for.what_they_did: Backed the rollback of runoff, wetlands, and permitting rules during the 1995 regulatory-reform push.

against.name: 150 of 203 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 150 to 45, and 159 of them backed the motion to recommit the bill.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Senate committee of referral (chaired by John Chafee, R-RI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 18, 1995, referred to the committee, and never reported it to the Senate floor.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and threatened to veto it as a weakening of the Clean Water Act.

against.name: Environmental and conservation groups
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill as the most serious attempt to weaken the Clean Water Act since its passage.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split sharply by party — 195 of 230 Republicans for passage versus 45 of 203 Democrats — and the motion to recommit split 159-37 among Democrats and 9-219 among Republicans.

industries.industry: Livestock and poultry operations (concentrated animal feeding operations)
industries.note: Land-applied manure would be enforced only as nonpoint source pollution, and CAFO waste lagoons would be excluded from regulated waters, with existing lagoons exempt no matter their size or capacity. That shifts waste-handling costs from the operations to the waters the public uses.

The wetlands title replaces the existing permit program with a three-tier system, exempts many agricultural and previously denied activities, and makes taxpayers compensate owners whenever wetland rules cut a property's value 20 percent or more — turning a public protection into a public expense.

Stormwater leaves the permit system, new standards face a cost-benefit veto and risk assessments, permits stretch from 5 to 10 years, plants get credits for pollutants already in their intake water, silver dischargers get pretreatment relief, and coal remining operations are deemed compliant under set conditions.

Cities gain up to 15-year compliance schedules for sewer overflows and a waiver letting some ocean outfalls count chemically enhanced primary treatment as secondary treatment, plus a $300 million grant authorization (contingent on a $2.25 billion loan-fund appropriation). Delayed fixes save ratepayers money now but leave overflows flowing longer.

The bill directs the Army Secretary to set up a mitigation banking program in every state and lets developers meet wetland losses through purchased credits, creating a new market. It can offset some losses but also lets protection of a wetland be swapped for a distant, possibly lesser one.
